category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Go to bed and get up at about the same times every day.
sourceWording: Maintain a consistent sleep schedule
paragraph: Set a regular bedtime and wake-up time, even on weekends. Use alarms or bedtime reminders to help stay consistent, and get morning sunlight to reinforce your body’s natural clock.
disagreements: Which matters more, a fixed bedtime or a fixed wake time

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: If you need to move your sleep times, shift them a little each day instead of all at once.
sourceWording: Avoid drastic changes in sleep and wake times
paragraph: Gradually adjust your sleep schedule by shifting your bedtime or wake-up time by 15–30 minutes per night instead of making sudden changes.
editorNotes: The wiki item title says 'avoid drastic changes'; its practical tip is about shifting 15-30 minutes per night, which is the actionable version used for the plain line.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Most adults need 7 to 9 hours; notice how much you need to wake up rested.
sourceWording: Follow the 8-hour rule
paragraph: Set a consistent bedtime and wake-up time, even on weekends.
audienceNote: The wiki taxonomy labels this '8-hour rule (recommended in Asia)'; the regional claim has no citation. Children and teens need more sleep than adults; that is not covered here.
editorNotes: Item name and its own evidence disagree. Suggest renaming the item; the plain line follows the evidence, not the title.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: If you nap, keep it short and before mid-afternoon.
sourceWording: Avoid long or irregular daytime naps
audienceNote: Napping norms differ by culture (siesta cultures, workplace naps). Shift workers may need longer naps; see adjust-to-night-shift-work.
editorNotes: Duplicate of wiki 3.2.1 (see notes there).

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Get up at the same time every day, weekends too.
sourceWording: Try a consistent wake-up time even on weekends
editorNotes: Listed in the wiki taxonomy with no write-up.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: On weekends, wake up within about an hour of your weekday time.
sourceWording: Limit social jet lag by maintaining weekday sleep patterns on weekends
disagreements: How much weekend sleep-in is OK
editorNotes: The wiki item says 'limit social jet lag'. The one-hour figure in the plain line is Huberman's and is unverified; see also myth M2.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Keep your bedroom cool and dark at night.
sourceWording: Keep your bedroom cool and dark
paragraph: Set your thermostat between 60–67°F (15–19°C) for optimal sleep. If you don’t have air conditioning, use a fan, breathable bedding, and light pajamas to stay cool.
audienceNote: Cooling tips assume a fan or air conditioning; hot climates and shared rooms make this harder.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Block light from windows with heavy curtains or an eye mask.
sourceWording: Use blackout curtains
paragraph: If blackout curtains are too expensive or impractical, try an eye mask to block out light.
editorNotes: Write-up has no citations.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Sleep on a mattress and pillow that feel comfortable to you.
sourceWording: Invest in a comfortable mattress and pillow
paragraph: If a new mattress isn’t an option, try a mattress topper for added comfort or a pillow suited to your sleep position (firm for side sleepers, softer for back sleepers).
editorNotes: Wiki name 'Invest in...' assumes money; the tip offers a mattress topper as a cheaper option. Write-up has no citations.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: If noise wakes you, try a fan or white noise to cover it.
sourceWording: Use white noise machines
paragraph: If a machine is not available, alternatives like a fan, air purifier, or low-volume static from a radio can provide a similar effect.
editorNotes: Overlaps 1.2.5 and 1.4.2 (pink noise). Write-up has no citations.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Make your bedroom as quiet as you can, or use earplugs.
sourceWording: Have it quiet
editorNotes: Wiki page is a blank template. Earplugs in the plain line are an editorial addition, not from a source.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Charge your phone and other devices outside the bedroom.
sourceWording: Remove electronic devices from the bedroom
editorNotes: Listed with no write-up. Related to 1.3.1; the NSF 2024 consensus found screen use harms sleep in children and teens, not adults (see 1.3.1).

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Keep your bedroom tidy so it feels calm.
sourceWording: Keep bedroom clutter-free for a more relaxing atmosphere
editorNotes: Listed with no write-up or evidence.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Try a calming scent such as lavender at bedtime.
sourceWording: Use aromatherapy with calming scents like lavender
editorNotes: Listed with no write-up or evidence.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: In the hour before bed, choose calm screen use or none, and keep phones out of children's bedrooms.
sourceWording: Avoid screens before bed
paragraph: Set a “screen curfew” 30–60 minutes before bed and switch to audiobooks, reading, or relaxation exercises instead. If you must use a screen, enable night mode or blue light filters.
audienceNote: The NSF 2024 consensus found harm in children and teens; it did not reach consensus for adults. Keep a separate adult wording until adult evidence is checked.
disagreements: How strong the evidence is, and for whom | Mechanism: light or content
editorNotes: This is the worked example in the Open Health Communication Declaration (vivwebsolutions/hcf-guides#6). The plain line is a first try at the nuanced version and needs Kalman's review. Wiki tip: a 'screen curfew' 30-60 minutes before bed.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Do the same calm things in the same order before bed, like reading or a warm shower.
sourceWording: Establish a relaxing bedtime routine (e.g., reading, warm bath)
paragraph: Create a 30-minute wind-down routine before bed with calming activities like reading, light stretching, or listening to soft music. Stick to the same routine nightly to reinforce your body's sleep signals.
editorNotes: Write-up has no citations.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Save exciting or stressful activities for earlier in the evening.
sourceWording: Reduce stimulating activities close to bedtime
paragraph: Avoid intense exercise, heavy discussions, or engaging TV shows at least 1 hour before bed. Instead, opt for calming activities like gentle stretching, journaling, or deep breathing exercises.
editorNotes: Overlaps 1.3.7 and 2.3.4. Write-up has no citations.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: If you wake at night, don't look at the clock.
sourceWording: Avoid checking the clock if you wake up at night – Clock-watching can increase stress and make it harder to fall back asleep.
paragraph: Turn your clock away from your bed or use a non-illuminated alarm clock. If you wake up, focus on relaxing breathing exercises rather than checking the time.
editorNotes: NHLBI (p. 30) says to turn the clock face away. Write-up has no citations.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Try a guided sleep meditation or a mindfulness recording at bedtime.
sourceWording: Try guided sleep meditations or mindfulness apps
editorNotes: Listed with no write-up. Overlaps 3.1.2.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Some people find a weighted blanket calming at night.
sourceWording: Use a weighted blanket for a calming effect
audienceNote: Not checked for children; weighted blankets carry safety warnings for infants and young children (warning not sourced here; check before publishing).
editorNotes: Listed with no write-up or evidence.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Leave hard conversations for earlier in the day when you can.
sourceWording: Avoid mentally stimulating discussions before bedtime
editorNotes: Listed with no write-up. Overlaps 1.3.3.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Take a warm bath or shower an hour or two before bed.
sourceWording: Take a warm shower or bath before bed – This helps cool your core body temperature post-shower, signaling sleep readiness.
paragraph: Take a warm bath or shower 60–90 minutes before bedtime for optimal results. Keep it lukewarm rather than too hot, and allow time for your body to cool down naturally.
editorNotes: Wiki scores ease 3 on the item page but 5 in both summary tables. Write-up has no citations.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: Some people sleep better with pink noise, like steady rain, than white noise.
sourceWording: Try pink noise instead of white noise – Pink noise (e.g., rustling leaves, steady rain) has been shown to enhance deep sleep.
paragraph: Use free apps or YouTube to find pink noise sounds, or try a white noise machine with a pink noise setting. Experiment with different soundscapes to find what works best for you.
editorNotes: Wiki's own scores disagree sharply on evidence (item page: 'well supported'; classification table: 'weak evidence', impact 1). Write-up has no citations.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
plain: If your feet get cold, wear loose socks to bed.
sourceWording: Sleep with socks on – Keeping your feet warm helps dilate blood vessels, signaling to the body that it's time to sleep.
paragraph: Wear loose, breathable socks or place a hot water bottle near your feet to keep them warm without overheating.
editorNotes: Pulls the opposite way from cooling tips (1.2.1, frozen water bottle); the wiki says warm feet help the body shed heat. Write-up has no citations.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
subcategory: Light Exposure and Circadian Rhythm Regulation
plain: Get outside in daylight soon after you wake up.
sourceWording: Morning sunlight exposure
paragraph: Spend 10–30 minutes outside in the morning, preferably within an hour of waking. If natural sunlight isn’t available, consider using a bright light therapy lamp for similar benefits.
audienceNote: Hard for people who wake before sunrise, in high-latitude winters, or who can't go outside.
editorNotes: Wiki scores reach 3 on the item page but 5 in the summary table, and novelty 4 vs 1.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
subcategory: Light Exposure and Circadian Rhythm Regulation
plain: Use dimmer, warmer lights in the evening.
sourceWording: Reduce blue light exposure in the evening
paragraph: Use blue light filter apps on screens, wear blue light-blocking glasses, and switch to warm, dim lighting (like red or amber bulbs) 1–2 hours before bed.
editorNotes: Wiki item says 'reduce blue light'. The NSF 2024 consensus did not reach consensus that pre-bedtime screen light impairs sleep; the plain line is about room light overall, not screen filters. Write-up has no citations.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
subcategory: Light Exposure and Circadian Rhythm Regulation
plain: If you need light at night, use a dim red or amber one.
sourceWording: Use dim red light at night instead of blue or white light – Red light has the least impact on melatonin production and circadian rhythm.
paragraph: Use a red night light or replace bedside lamps with dim red bulbs in the evening to minimize sleep disruption.
editorNotes: Wiki scores disagree on evidence (item page: well supported; classification table: limited). Huberman's reason (cortisol) is unverified. Write-up has no citations.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
subcategory: Light Exposure and Circadian Rhythm Regulation
plain: Turn the lights down little by little as bedtime gets closer.
sourceWording: Use smart lighting to gradually dim before bed
editorNotes: Wiki item names 'smart lighting'; the plain line drops the product. Listed with no write-up.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
subcategory: Light Exposure and Circadian Rhythm Regulation
plain: Some people wear blue-light-blocking glasses in the evening.
sourceWording: Wear blue-light-blocking glasses in the evening
editorNotes: Listed with no write-up or evidence. See 2.1.2 for why the light mechanism is disputed.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Have your last caffeine by early afternoon and your last big meal a few hours before bed.
sourceWording: Avoid caffeine and heavy meals before bed
paragraph: Avoid caffeine at least 6 hours before bed and finish heavy meals 2–3 hours before sleeping. If hungry late at night, opt for a light snack like yogurt or a banana.
editorNotes: NHLBI pairs caffeine with nicotine; the wiki has no nicotine item. Wiki splits alcohol into 2.2.3.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Drink most of your fluids earlier in the day so you don't wake up to use the bathroom.
sourceWording: Stay hydrated earlier in the day and gradually reduce water intake
paragraph: Drink most of your fluids in the morning and afternoon, then slow down in the evening to reduce nighttime disruptions.
audienceNote: Not for people who need fluids at night for medicine, diabetes or thirst (caution from the glossary's 3-2-1 entry).

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Don't use alcohol to help you sleep; stop drinking a few hours before bed.
sourceWording: Avoid alcohol close to bedtime as it disrupts sleep cycles
editorNotes: Listed with no write-up; myth M1 covers the same ground with citations. '3 hours' is from the 3-2-1 rule, not a trial.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Eat foods with enough magnesium; ask before taking a supplement.
sourceWording: Ensure sufficient magnesium intake, which helps relax muscles
editorNotes: Listed with no write-up or evidence. Supplement safety not checked.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Be active most days; it helps you sleep better.
sourceWording: Regular exercise improves sleep quality
paragraph: Engage in at least 30 minutes of moderate exercise (e.g., walking, cycling, or strength training) most days, but avoid vigorous workouts right before bed, as they may be too stimulating.
editorNotes: NHLBI: at least 30 minutes most days (p. 28).

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Try a few minutes of gentle stretching or yoga before bed.
sourceWording: Try relaxing exercises like yoga or stretching before bed
paragraph: Try 5–10 minutes of gentle stretching or yoga poses, such as child’s pose, forward bend, or deep breathing exercises, to help relax the body before bed.
editorNotes: Write-up has no citations.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: If you do strength training, try it in the afternoon or early evening.
sourceWording: Try resistance training in the afternoon – Strength training earlier in the day has been linked to improved deep sleep quality.
paragraph: Aim for 30–45 minutes of resistance training in the afternoon or early evening, such as bodyweight exercises, weightlifting, or resistance bands, to maximize deep sleep benefits.
editorNotes: Wiki scores disagree (classification table: reach 1, novelty 5; item page: reach 2, novelty 4). Write-up has no citations.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Finish hard workouts at least a couple of hours before bed.
sourceWording: Avoid intense workouts within 2 hours of bedtime

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: To wind down, breathe in for 4, hold for 7, and breathe out for 8.
sourceWording: Practice the 4-7-8 breathing technique before bed – Inhaling for 4 seconds, holding for 7, and exhaling for 8 can slow heart rate and promote relaxation.
paragraph: Before bed, try four cycles of the 4-7-8 breathing technique while lying down in a comfortable position to help calm the nervous system.
editorNotes: Wiki item says it 'can slow heart rate'; the glossary flags Breus's heart-rate claim as unverified. Write-up has no citations.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Mouth taping is popular, but the evidence is thin; check with a clinician first.
sourceWording: Sleep with your mouth closed (or use mouth tape if needed) – Mouth breathing at night can reduce oxygen efficiency and disrupt sleep quality.
paragraph: If you struggle with mouth breathing, try nasal strips or practice breathing exercises during the day to strengthen nasal breathing habits before considering mouth tape.
editorNotes: Wiki rates evidence weak-to-limited and impact low in its classification tables, but well supported on the item page. Safety for people with blocked noses or possible sleep apnea not checked; the plain line is cautious on purpose. The wiki's novelty-vs-reach section calls mouth taping 'strong scientific support but low commonality', which contradicts its own scores.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Try slow breathing through your nose before sleep.
sourceWording: Try nasal breathing exercises before sleep
editorNotes: Listed with no write-up.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Some small studies found kiwi or tart cherry before bed helped sleep.
sourceWording: Consume kiwi or tart cherries before bed – Both are rich in sleep-promoting compounds like serotonin and melatonin.
paragraph: Eat one kiwi or a small serving of tart cherry juice about an hour before bed to naturally boost melatonin and improve sleep quality.
editorNotes: Plain line hedged because the wiki write-up cites no studies and its classification table rates evidence 'limited'. Availability and cost vary by region.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: If you're hungry at bedtime, a small snack is fine.
sourceWording: Eat a small, carb-rich snack 30 minutes before bed – A banana with almond butter can trigger serotonin production, aiding sleep.
paragraph: Try a small snack like a banana with almond butter or whole-grain crackers with cheese about 30 minutes before bed to support relaxation and sleep onset.
editorNotes: Wiki's serotonin reasoning is uncited.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: A cup of chamomile tea can be part of a calm bedtime routine.
sourceWording: Drink chamomile or passionflower tea before bed – These herbal teas have mild sedative effects that promote relaxation.
paragraph: Drink a cup of chamomile or passionflower tea about 30–45 minutes before bed to help relax and prepare for sleep.
audienceNote: Herbal products can interact with medicines; passionflower especially (not sourced here; check).
editorNotes: Wiki summary table rates evidence 5/5; item page rates it 'well supported'; the write-up cites nothing.

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Do something that calms you before bed when you're stressed.
sourceWording: Manage stress and anxiety before sleep
paragraph: Try deep breathing, journaling, or progressive muscle relaxation before bed to calm the mind and reduce nighttime stress.
editorNotes: Broad; 3.1.2-3.1.4 are the specific ways to do it.

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Try slow breathing or meditation to relax at bedtime.
sourceWording: Practice relaxation techniques (e.g., deep breathing, meditation)
paragraph: Try the 4-7-8 breathing technique before bed: inhale for 4 seconds, hold for 7 seconds, and exhale for 8 seconds to promote relaxation and prepare for sleep.
editorNotes: Write-up has no citations.

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Tense and then relax each muscle group, one at a time, from feet to head.
sourceWording: Use progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) before bed – Tensing and relaxing muscle groups one by one can reduce physical tension and improve sleep onset.
paragraph: Start with your feet and work your way up, tensing each muscle group for 5-10 seconds, then relaxing for 15-20 seconds to promote full-body relaxation before sleep.

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep
placement: listed in the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' (not yet placed)
plain: Write down what's on your mind, and one next step, before bed.
sourceWording: Write down worries or concerns before bed to clear your mind
editorNotes: In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list (not yet placed). No write-up.

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Short naps are fine for most people; long or late naps can make night sleep harder.
sourceWording: Naps harm nighttime sleep
paragraph: If you nap, keep it under 30 minutes and avoid napping after 3 PM to minimize its impact on nighttime sleep.
editorNotes: The wiki item is a claim ('Naps harm nighttime sleep'), not advice, and its own evidence says it depends. Recommend merging into 1.1.4 and moving the claim to the myths list.

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Use your bed only for sleep and sex.
sourceWording: Use the bed only for sleep and intimacy
paragraph: If you can’t sleep after 20 minutes, get out of bed and do a relaxing activity (e.g., reading under dim light) until you feel sleepy, then return to bed.
editorNotes: Part of stimulus control (NHLBI calls it reconditioning therapy). Wiki tip folds in 3.2.3.

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep
placement: listed in the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' (not yet placed)
plain: If you can't sleep after about 20 minutes, get up and do something calm until you feel sleepy.
sourceWording: Avoid lying in bed awake for more than 20 minutes—get up and do a calming activity
disagreements: Get up or stay in bed
editorNotes: Direct conflict between sources; the declaration's 'where sources disagree' field exists for cases like this. In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list. No write-up.

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: If your mind races, picture a string of random, unconnected things.
sourceWording: Engage in "cognitive shuffling" – Randomly think of unrelated words or images to prevent overthinking and induce sleep faster.
paragraph: Try mentally listing random objects that aren’t connected (e.g., apple, ladder, river, violin) to disengage from stressful thoughts and ease into sleep.
editorNotes: Kept on purpose as niche-but-maybe-valuable (Kalman's v1.2 feedback). Wiki scores clash: classification table rates evidence 1 (weakest), item page rates it well supported, and the scatterplot text promotes it as 'practical but lesser-known'. Write-up has no citations.

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Before bed, write down three things you're thankful for.
sourceWording: Use a gratitude journal instead of a to-do list – Writing down positive things before bed can reduce stress and improve sleep onset.
paragraph: Each night, write down three things you’re grateful for and why—this shifts focus away from stress and promotes relaxation before bed.
editorNotes: Wiki item says 'instead of a to-do list', which conflicts with 3.1.4 (write down worries and next steps). Write-up has no citations.

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep
plain: Some people relax with binaural beats; evidence for sleep is mixed.
sourceWording: Listen to binaural beats at a sleep-friendly frequency (e.g., 2-8 Hz) – Some studies suggest they may promote deep relaxation and sleep.
paragraph: Try delta wave binaural beats (2-4 Hz) for deep sleep by listening through stereo headphones at low volume before bed.
editorNotes: Needs headphones. Wiki rates it 3 on red flags (mixed) on the item page. Write-up has no citations.

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep
placement: listed in the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' (not yet placed)
plain: Try nature sounds or ASMR recordings to relax at bedtime.
sourceWording: Listen to nature sounds or ASMR for relaxation
editorNotes: In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list. No write-up.

category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
plain: If you get heartburn at night, try sleeping on your left side.
sourceWording: Sleep on your left side to aid digestion and reduce acid reflux – This can be beneficial for people with GERD or heartburn issues.
paragraph: If you experience acid reflux at night, try placing a wedge pillow under your upper body while sleeping on your left side for added relief.
editorNotes: Wiki summary table rates evidence 5/5; write-up cites nothing. Pregnancy advice about left-side sleeping is a separate topic, not covered.

category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
plain: Some people relax with gentle massage or acupressure before sleep.
sourceWording: Try acupressure or gentle massage before sleep – Specific pressure points (like the pericardium-6 point on the wrist) have been linked to relaxation and better sleep.
paragraph: Try gently massaging the pericardium-6 point (three finger-widths below your wrist crease) in circular motions for one to two minutes before bed to promote relaxation.
audienceNote: Acupressure points (P6) come from traditional Chinese medicine.
editorNotes: Write-up has no citations.

category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
plain: If you have reflux or sleep apnea, raising your upper body may help; ask your clinician.
sourceWording: Try an inclined sleeping position if you have sleep apnea or acid reflux – A slight elevation (e.g., using a wedge pillow) can improve breathing and digestion.
paragraph: For best results, elevate your upper body by 6-8 inches using a wedge pillow or an adjustable bed instead of stacking pillows, which can strain the neck.
editorNotes: Wiki classification tables rate it 1 on everything (hardest, weakest); the item page rates it well supported with strong impact. Biggest internal spread in the wiki.

category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
placement: listed in the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' (not yet placed)
plain: Some people find raising their legs a little helps them feel comfortable at night.
sourceWording: Elevate your legs slightly to improve circulation
editorNotes: In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list. No write-up or evidence; the circulation claim in the wiki title is not repeated.

category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
plain: Write down when you go to bed, wake up and how you slept for a week or two.
sourceWording: Keep a sleep diary to track patterns and identify issues – Helpful for diagnosing sleep disorders or making adjustments to improve sleep quality.
paragraph: Use a notebook or sleep-tracking app to record your bedtime, wake time, sleep interruptions, and factors like caffeine intake or stress levels for at least two weeks to spot trends.
editorNotes: A sleep diary is the starting point for sleep restriction therapy and CBT-I. Write-up has no citations.

category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
plain: If you can't fall asleep until very late, ask a clinician about morning bright-light therapy.
sourceWording: Consider light therapy if you have delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD) – A bright light box in the morning can help reset the body’s internal clock.
paragraph: If you struggle with falling asleep late and waking up late, use a 10,000-lux light box for 30 minutes within an hour of waking up to help regulate your circadian rhythm.
editorNotes: Wiki tip names a 10,000-lux box. Write-up has no citations.

category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
placement: listed in the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' (not yet placed)
plain: Melatonin may help with jet lag or shift work; ask a pharmacist or doctor first.
sourceWording: Consider a melatonin supplement if struggling with jet lag or shift work
audienceNote: Melatonin is sold over the counter in some countries and by prescription in others.
editorNotes: In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list. No write-up.

category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
placement: listed in the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' (not yet placed)
plain: If you snore loudly or gasp in your sleep, ask a doctor about sleep apnea.
sourceWording: Check for potential sleep apnea
editorNotes: In the wiki's 'New Sleep Advices' list. No write-up; myth M5 (snoring) covers it with citations. The glossary has 'Sleep Apnea, Central' but no obstructive sleep apnea term yet.

category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
placement: proposed (glossary entry, not in the wiki taxonomy)
plain: Ask your pharmacist or doctor whether any of your medicines can affect sleep.
sourceWording: Review Medicines That Disrupt Sleep
paragraph: Some heart, blood pressure, and asthma medicines, along with some over-the-counter cough, cold, and allergy remedies, can interfere with sleep. If you're having trouble sleeping, ask your doctor or pharmacist whether something you're taking could be the cause, and whether it can be taken earlier in the day instead.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note

category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
placement: proposed (glossary entry, not in the wiki taxonomy)
plain: For long-lasting insomnia, ask about CBT-I, a structured talking and habits treatment.
sourceWording: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia
paragraph: A structured treatment for chronic insomnia that combines behavior changes — like reconditioning and sleep restriction therapy — with replacing unhelpful thoughts about sleep, such as "I'll never fall asleep without pills," with more realistic ones. It's effective for most people with chronic insomnia.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note
editorNotes: The wiki's discussion tab names CBT-I as the intervention linking categories 3 and 4, but it has no item.

category: Medical and Pharmacological Considerations
placement: proposed (glossary entry, not in the wiki taxonomy)
plain: With a clinician's help, limit time in bed to the sleep you actually get, then add time back.
sourceWording: Sleep Restriction Therapy
paragraph: A technique for insomnia that limits time in bed to match how much you actually sleep. Calculate your average sleep time over a week, keep your time in bed to that amount, then gradually add more as your sleep improves. Naps longer than 15-20 minutes are avoided during this process, since they can undo the effect.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note
editorNotes: NHLBI caution: avoid driving or machinery while sleep-deprived during this process.

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
placement: proposed (glossary entry, not in the wiki taxonomy)
plain: Before a long trip, shift your sleep times a little toward the new time zone.
sourceWording: Coping With Jet Lag
paragraph: A handful of adjustments that can ease jet lag on a trip of more than a few days: shift your sleep and wake times by small steps for a couple of days beforehand, get plenty of outdoor daylight right after you arrive, skip alcohol and afternoon caffeine, and keep any naps short (10-15 minutes).
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)
placement: proposed (glossary entry, not in the wiki taxonomy)
plain: On night shifts, use bright light at work and a dark, quiet room to sleep in.
sourceWording: Adjusting to Night Shift Work
paragraph: Ways to make night-shift sleep easier: add naps and extra sleep time, use bright light at work, keep shift changes infrequent so your body clock has time to adjust, block out light and noise while sleeping during the day, and limit caffeine to the start of the shift.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
subcategory: Light Exposure and Circadian Rhythm Regulation
placement: proposed (glossary entry, not in the wiki taxonomy)
plain: Some advise getting outside in late-afternoon light too.
sourceWording: Late-Afternoon Sunlight Viewing
paragraph: Spend a little time outdoors in the late afternoon or early evening, when the sun is low, looking toward the sky (never straight at the sun). It is meant to signal to your body clock that evening is coming.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note
editorNotes: Huberman only; low confidence in the glossary. His protective claim is unverified and left out.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep
subcategory: Light Exposure and Circadian Rhythm Regulation
placement: proposed (glossary entry, not in the wiki taxonomy)
plain: Your body is coldest a couple of hours before you usually wake.
sourceWording: Temperature Minimum
paragraph: The coldest point of your body's daily temperature cycle. In this model it falls about 2 hours before you usually wake up, so about 5 a.m. if you wake at 7. Bright light, exercise, or caffeine in the 2 to 4 hours before it nudges your body clock later; the same things in the hours just after it nudge your clock earlier. Some people use the timing to shift their clock before travel.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note
editorNotes: A concept used in jet-lag advice, not advice by itself. The 2-hour figure is Huberman's and unverified.

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

plain: Breathe in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4, and repeat.
sourceWording: Box Breathing
paragraph: A counted breathing pattern: breathe in for 4, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4, then repeat. Picturing the numbers as you count gives your mind something to focus on. Beginners can start with 4 to 5 rounds.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

plain: Breathe in fully through your nose, then breathe out slowly and completely.
sourceWording: Cyclic Sighing
paragraph: A breathing pattern for calming down fast: breathe in through the nose until your lungs feel full, then, without holding, let the air out slowly and completely. A few rounds is often enough to quiet racing thoughts.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

plain: Breathe slowly so your belly, not your chest, rises and falls.
sourceWording: Belly Breathing
paragraph: Breathing deeply so your belly rises as you breathe in and falls as you breathe out, slowly and through the nose. It is the base skill for most other relaxation breathing exercises.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

plain: Breathe in through one nostril and out the other, switching sides.
sourceWording: Alternate Nostril Breathing
paragraph: A breathing exercise where you close one nostril with a finger, breathe in through the other, then switch sides for the breath out and the next breath in. Beginners can try 5 to 10 rounds. It is used to settle strong emotions.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note

category: Psychological and Emotional Factors Affecting Sleep

plain: If you can't sleep, lying still with your eyes closed still rests your body.
sourceWording: Non-Sleep Deep Rest
paragraph: Lying still in the dark and quiet, awake, with your eyes closed. It is not sleep, but it can still rest the body, which can take pressure off the effort to fall asleep.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note
editorNotes: Pulls against 3.2.3 (get up after 20 minutes).

category: Sleep Hygiene (General Behavioral and Environmental Factors)

plain: Use the last hour before bed for chores, then washing up, then something calm.
sourceWording: Power-Down Hour
paragraph: A set hour before bed split into three 20-minute parts: one for chores and last-minute tasks, one for hygiene such as brushing teeth, washing your face, or a warm shower, and one for something slow and calming such as reading, meditation, or prayer. Setting an alarm an hour before bedtime reminds you to start.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note

category: Physiological and Biological Factors Affecting Sleep

plain: Stop alcohol 3 hours, food 2 hours and drinks 1 hour before bed.
sourceWording: 3-2-1 Rule
paragraph: A countdown before bed: stop alcohol 3 hours before, stop eating 2 hours before, and stop drinking fluids 1 hour before. People who need fluids for medicine, diabetes, or constant thirst should skip the fluid cutoff and ask their doctor.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note
audienceNote: Skip the fluid step if you need fluids for medicine, diabetes or thirst.

sourceWording: Cool Down With a Frozen Water Bottle
paragraph: A low-tech way to cool your body before sleep: freeze a bottle of water, put it in a sock, and place one by each hip in bed.

paragraph: Drink water first and wait about 90 minutes after waking before your first cup of coffee.

sourceWording: Set a Caffeine Cutoff
paragraph: Pick a time in the early afternoon after which you stop caffeine, so it has worn off by bedtime. Caffeine can stay in your body for many hours.

plain: If you're naturally a night owl or early bird, set your bedtime with that in mind.
sourceWording: Match Bedtime to Your Chronotype
paragraph: Your chronotype is your natural lean toward mornings or evenings. Going to bed much earlier or later than your body prefers can make falling asleep harder, so set your bedtime with your own pattern in mind.

plain: One expert says to stay in bed and breathe slowly when you wake at night.
sourceWording: Stay in Bed and Breathe When You Wake at Night
paragraph: When you wake in the middle of the night, stay in bed with the lights off and use slow breathing to settle, instead of getting up, walking around, or picking up your phone. If you do not need the bathroom, skip the trip. Keep a glass of room-temperature water by the bed.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note

plain: After dark, keep indoor lights low and screens dim.
sourceWording: Dim the Lights at Night
paragraph: After sunset, keep indoor lighting low. Avoid bright overhead lights, especially from about 10 p.m. to 4 a.m., turn screens down as far as you can still use them, and use only as much light as you need to move around safely.
evidenceStatus: no evidence summary; see glossary review note
editorNotes: Overlaps 2.1.2 and 2.1.4. Huberman's 10 p.m.-4 a.m. window is his rule of thumb.

category: Busting sleep myths
plain: Alcohol may make you drowsy, but it makes sleep worse later in the night.
sourceWording: Myth: Alcohol helps you sleep better.
paragraph: While alcohol may induce drowsiness and help you fall asleep faster, it negatively impacts the quality of your rest[77][78].

category: Busting sleep myths
plain: Sleeping in on weekends doesn't fully make up for short sleep during the week.
sourceWording: Myth: You can "catch up" on lost sleep during weekends.
paragraph: Sleeping in on weekends may provide temporary relief from sleep deprivation, but it does not fully restore the negative effects of lost sleep[82][83].

category: Busting sleep myths
plain: Regular exercise helps sleep, but hard workouts right before bed can keep you up.
sourceWording: Myth: Exercising right before bed improves sleep.
paragraph: Regular exercise is well known for promoting better sleep by reducing stress, improving mood, and regulating the body's circadian rhythm[17]. However, engaging in intense workouts too close to bedtime can have the opposite effect.

category: Busting sleep myths
plain: Falling asleep to TV can make sleep lighter and more broken.
sourceWording: Myth: Watching TV helps you fall asleep.
paragraph: Many people believe that watching TV before bed helps them unwind and fall asleep, but it can actually do more harm than good[88].
editorNotes: Wiki explains this with blue light; see 1.3.1 for why the light mechanism is disputed.

category: Busting sleep myths
plain: Loud, frequent snoring can be a sign of sleep apnea and is worth checking.
sourceWording: Myth: Snoring is harmless.
paragraph: Occasional snoring is common and may result from factors like nasal congestion, sleep position, or fatigue[89][90]. However, frequent and loud snoring can be a warning sign of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), a serious sleep disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep[91].
